video.title: Why You Should Start Your Swing at Contact

classification.reason: The coach provides actionable mental cues including 'the swing starts at contact' and 'accelerate all the way to contact', along with a specific frame-counting video audit method.

problem.title_as_question: Why Should You Start Your Swing at Contact?
problem.definition: Players often decelerate their hand prematurely before contact, releasing the wrist's elastic stretch too early and losing both effortless power and directional control.

symptoms.description: The ball comes off slower and loses the effortless crack feeling.
Shots are sprayed and directional control is lost.
The wrist lag releases prematurely, with the racket overtaking the hand 5 to 6 frames before contact on 60 fps video.
Player feels the need to actively flex the wrist and manipulate the racket face with muscular effort.

causes.statement: Players intuitively assume a long delay exists between hand deceleration and ball contact, causing them to decelerate their hand prematurely.
The forward acceleration of the arm and hand stops too far from the ball instead of continuing right up to contact, causing the wrist spring to release early.
Because the spring released before the ball arrived, the brain actively flexes and manipulates the racket using slow-twitch muscles to preserve the string angle.
Elastic energy stored in the wrist leaks out linearly with each millisecond the release window is extended beyond the optimal 40-millisecond duration.

angles.summary: On the modern forehand, the hitting action is an elastic spring release of roughly 40 milliseconds where the racket rapidly overtakes the hand three frames before contact at 60 fps.
The delay between spring release and contact is so tiny (0.04 seconds) that it should feel physically simultaneous with contact.
Elite pros like Federer, Alcaraz, Raducanu, and Rybakina consistently maintain full wrist lag until exactly three frames before contact at 60 fps.
A student progressed from an inefficient 12-frame release window at 120 fps to a clean, elastic 5-to-6 frame window that produced effortless power.
Players wrongly intuit that they must stop accelerating their hand long before striking the ball rather than driving forward right up to contact.

solutions.summary: Audit video at 60 fps by stepping back three frames from contact using the keyboard to check if the wrist lag release begins roughly three frames before contact.
solutions.external_goal: Check video frame count from contact at 60 fps

solutions.summary: Adopt the mental cue that 'the swing starts at contact' to eliminate the perceived delay and prevent early deceleration.
Intuit the swing as accelerating the hand all the way into contact rather than trying to micromanage the 0.04-second release timing window.
Sustain forward acceleration right next to the ball by pressing with the chest, rotating the hips, and maintaining a strong base before allowing the racket to snap.
